The Third Part of my humble work Nameless Heroes—"Behind-the-Lines Operations at Shanghai in the War of Resistance against Japan" (a tentative title)—is soon to appear by installments in Biographical Literature. This book recounts the astonishing deeds of slaying the foe and rooting out traitors wrought by the "Shanghai District" under my "Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Military Affairs Commission" in the years of the War of Resistance. In the "Prefatory Candour" of the First Part of Nameless Heroes, Rooting Out Traitors in the North, it was already mentioned: "The book of the Third Part chiefly recounts how, in the space of a little more than two years, from the eighth month of the twenty-eighth year to the tenth month of the thirtieth year, the comrades of the 'Shanghai District,' one and all devoted to their charge, brought off great deeds of the utmost foe-destroying power."

In the last two years I have heard, one after another, the views and reactions of certain old comrades of the former "Shanghai District," who take a particular interest in the persons and events the book is to treat—above all those touching themselves, such as the ins and outs of the action-cases. Broadly, their attitudes may be divided into three kinds: some hold that a light touch will suffice, and that there is no need to paint in detail; some earnestly enjoin me by no means to name names; and some, on the contrary, hope that their year's sacrifice and struggle in those days may not be buried and lost, and that the fuller and more detailed the writing, the better. Of course, more than forty years having passed, each man's situation now differs, and each must surely have his own reasons; and the writer ought to show them especial respect. Yet—"the tree rises from its root, and the water comes from its source." In writing this sort of essay, the great thing is to be faithful to the historical facts, and to hold up the loyal and the martyred to honor; and at times one cannot but set out clearly the true face of things, the whole course from head to tail. This is the first point on which I ask indulgence. The working comrades of the "Shanghai District" in those years numbered a thousand souls; and setting aside those who have died of age or illness and those trapped on the mainland, the number of them now living in Taiwan or sojourning in various places abroad is still not small, and most, moreover, have fallen out of contact, so that it is hard indeed to seek out each one's honored opinion. This is the second point on which I ask indulgence. For these reasons I publish this short notice on purpose, in the hope that you will not grudge me your instruction, so that failings and omissions may happily be avoided. And should you be able to furnish any relevant material, to make good what I have failed to reach, that above all I should be most grateful for!
Letters may be sent to the "Biographical Literature Magazine Office," to be passed on to me, and that will serve.
Chen Gongshu, respectfully, the fifth month of the seventy-second year.
